processing: A needle-shaped green tea; the specific steps are not well documented. As with other needle greens, the leaf is fixed by heat and then shaped into straight strands before drying.
harvest_season: Not well documented for this tea; needle-shaped greens are typically made from early spring buds.
appearance_dry: Needle-shaped green strands, the shape that gives the tea its name.
appearance_liquor: Typical of bud-heavy Chinese greens, a pale, clear yellow-green.
appearance_wet: Typical of needle greens, tender buds or young shoots of a soft green.
taste_profile: Few tasting descriptions exist; bud-heavy Chinese spring greens are typically delicate, fresh and lightly sweet.

brewing.notes: General guidance for needle-shaped green teas: a glass shows off the leaf, and water around 80 C keeps the buds from stewing.

vintage_note: Usual for its class: sold as current-year spring green tea and best drunk within the year. It sits under the Ziyang selenium tea name, so a pack should name both the product and the harvest.
description:
Ziyang Yinzhen, Ziyang Silver Needle, is a needle-shaped green tea from Ziyang county in southern Shaanxi. It is one of the named products under Ziyang selenium tea, alongside Ziyang Maojian and Ziyang Cuifeng. It is not related to the Fujian white tea called Silver Needle, which shares only the name.

Little is documented about how this one is made. What can be said is what is typical of needle greens in general: young material, heat to stop oxidation, and careful shaping into straight strands.

Descriptions of its taste are just as scarce, so go by the class and expect something delicate and fresh with a gentle sweetness. Keep the water cool and brew it in a glass if you enjoy watching the leaf.

When buying, ask for the harvest date and make sure it is the Shaanxi green tea you are getting. Some writing uses Ziyang tea and Ziyang Yinzhen interchangeably, which adds to the confusion.
history: Little is documented about this tea on its own. It appears as a product within the Ziyang selenium tea family, whose name has been protected since the 2000s, but who first made it and when is not well recorded.
